title: The Gita in your week · one verse per day going forward
hook: the reading is done; the carrying starts
tomorrow: Gita path in the world: Gandhi, Thoreau, Tilak, Vivekananda

segments.voice: Yesterday: shloka, your twelve verses, the ones that stayed. Your line was yours. Did you write one down where you'd see it this morning? Today, what to do with them next. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

People who finish a marathon often say the strangest part is the Monday after. For months, every morning had a shape: the run, the plan, the number. Then it's done, and the morning is suddenly empty. Some people never run again. Others find a small, steady habit that keeps the thing alive. Tomorrow and the next day finish this camp. But the Gita wasn't written to be finished. In Hindu tradition it's read again, and again, for a lifetime. So today is about the Monday after.
screen: `THE MONDAY AFTER THE MARATHON.` → `THE MORNING SUDDENLY EMPTY.` → `A SMALL, STEADY HABIT.`

segments.voice: Hindu tradition has a word for this: svadhyaya. Sva, your own; adhyaya, study, reading, recitation. Self-study. It's older than the Gita, and the Gita names it twice. In chapter sixteen it's one of the divine qualities. In chapter seventeen, the discipline of speech includes the regular recitation of sacred texts. The yoga tradition later lists svadhyaya among its daily observances too. So reading isn't something you do once. It's a practice, like the sit. Here's a simple shape for the week. Take your twelve verses and give each day one. Monday, the self that never dies. Tuesday, your right is to the action. Wednesday, the lamp. Whatever your twelve are. Read the verse in the morning. Carry it through the day. At night, ask: where did it show up? After twelve days, start again. The same verses will say different things in a different month. That's normal. The Gita itself circles back: letting go of the fruit comes up in chapter two, again in three, again in five, and once more in eighteen. There are older rhythms too. Some families read one chapter a day, finishing the Gita in eighteen days. Some recite a chapter on a set day each week. Many temples and homes celebrate Gita Jayanti, the Gita's birthday, each winter in the month of Margashirsha, often with a full recitation. You can join any of these, or just keep one verse a day. The point is the carrying. The Gita becomes yours not when you finish it, but when a line of it turns up uninvited, halfway through a hard phone call. That's the word today: the Gita in your week.
screen: `SVADHYAYA: YOUR OWN STUDY.` · `ONE VERSE A DAY.` · `A CHAPTER A DAY, OR GITA JAYANTI.` · `IT SHOWS UP UNINVITED.` · then, large: `THE GITA IN YOUR WEEK.`

segments.voice: Sit, and choose tomorrow's verse. Just one, from your twelve. Let it come to mind in your own words. Then picture tomorrow: waking, the first hour, the hardest meeting, dinner, the drive home. Place the verse somewhere in that day, like leaving a note in a coat pocket for yourself to find. Then rest, and let it wait there. The bell holds the time.
Svadhyaya, one's own study. One verse a day, read in the morning, carried all day, and started again when the twelve are done.
Your line: carry. Tonight, before sleep, say tomorrow's verse once. In the morning, say it again. Then carry it. Day two hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Hindus read or recite the Gita regularly: a few verses each morning, a chapter a day across eighteen days, or a full recitation on Gita Jayanti in the month of Margashirsha; svadhyaya, one's own study of sacred texts, is counted as a spiritual discipline.

original.note: Sanskrit: svadhyaya, one's own (sva) study or recitation (adhyaya) of sacred texts; Gita 16.1 and 17.15.

trapdoor: what you thought: you read a holy book once, like a novel.
what it means: in Hindu practice it's read again and again, a verse or a chapter at a time, for a lifetime.
what a scholar hears: svadhyaya appears in Gita 16.1 and 17.15 ('svadhyaya-abhyasanam') and among the niyamas in Yoga Sutra 2.32; Gita Jayanti falls on Mokshada Ekadashi in Margashirsha.
